idiom_name: hand-written column descriptor tables (X-macro field lists + offsetof)
implementation_notes: C has neither reflection nor a dominant ORM, so both halves of the pattern are hand-built: the metadata store is a static array of column descriptors (column name, byte offset into the struct, size or type tag) produced by an X-macro field list, and the reader is macro expansion plus offsetof, which the compiler folds into constants. The mapping engine is a small class-agnostic binder that walks a descriptor array and calls the driver accessor (sqlite3_column_int, sqlite3_column_text, PQgetvalue) while writing through (char *)obj + offset; this is the classic structure in its manual form. It remains the right call for fixed-schema records in embedded and systems code, where a descriptor table removes the field-by-field copy loop; once the schema varies per deployment or the graph grows pointers, a generated accessor layer or a language with reflection is cheaper than extending the tables.
pitfalls: offsetof descriptors only work for flat structs: pointer members are stored by pointer, so the mapper must state who owns the string and when it is copied.
Nothing checks the descriptor order against the SELECT list - a column added in SQL without a matching descriptor silently shifts values into the wrong fields.
sizeof on a bit-field, flexible-array member or incomplete type is invalid, so such fields cannot be described this way at all.
There is no type safety: a descriptor whose type tag disagrees with the column's storage class converts garbage (reading a SQL NULL as an int is the classic case).
